summaries.summary: This clinical trial is studying a medication called deferasirox to see if it can help remove excess iron from the body in patients with certain blood disorders, such as leukemia or lymphoma, who have received multiple blood transfusions. The trial aims to determine if deferasirox can improve the body's immune function, reduce the risk of infections, and decrease the need for hospitalization or other medical interventions. Patients will take deferasirox orally once a day for up to 6 months to see if it can help reduce iron overload and improve their overall health.

This study is looking at how well two different hip replacement stems work. Fifty patients with degenerative joint disease, such as osteoarthritis, will be randomly assigned to receive one of the two stems. The study will track how the new hip moves over two years. To be in the study, patients must be between 18 and 70 years old, able to understand Dutch, and willing to come back for follow-up appointments. Patients with active infections, certain bone diseases, or neurological disorders may not be eligible.

This study is for patients with metastatic breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body and is not responsive to the HER2 protein. The goal of the study is to see how well a combination of two drugs, sorafenib and paclitaxel, works to slow or stop the growth of cancer cells. Patients will take sorafenib orally twice a day and receive paclitaxel through an IV every week for 3 weeks, then take a week off. This cycle will repeat every 4 weeks. The study will monitor how the cancer responds to the treatment, as well as any side effects that may occur. To be eligible, patients must have measurable disease, be at least 18 years old, and have a life expectancy of more than 6 months.

This study aims to improve the way antibiotics are prescribed in long-term care facilities. It wants to reduce the unnecessary use of antibiotics, which can lead to harmful side effects and antibiotic resistance. The study will use a method called audit-and-feedback to help doctors make better prescribing decisions. It will compare two different ways of providing feedback to doctors to see which one is more effective. The goal is to reduce the overuse of antibiotics, lower healthcare costs, and improve the health and safety of long-term care residents.

This study is testing a wearable device called the Biostrap wristband to see how well it measures heart function in patients who are having a cardiac ultrasound or a procedure to insert a special catheter in their heart. The device is worn on the wrist and uses a sensor to track heart activity. The study will compare the results from the wristband to the results from the standard medical tests. The goal is to see if the wristband can provide accurate and reliable information about heart function. The study is looking for 100 patients, aged 18 and older, who are having one of these medical tests. Participants will wear the wristband for either 1-2 hours or up to 7 days, depending on their situation.

This study aims to understand how people with certain muscle disorders, such as Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy, and a condition called osteogenesis imperfecta, interact with others and understand their own emotions and body. The study will compare these individuals with people who do not have these conditions. Participants will complete questionnaires and tasks, such as identifying emotions and measuring their comfort with personal space, and will wear a special headset to measure their brain activity while they rest. The goal is to learn more about social cognition, or how people understand and interact with others, in these conditions and to see if there are any differences in brain activity. The study is looking for participants with these conditions, as well as healthy volunteers, aged 4 and up.

This study compares two types of laxatives, Sennoside A+B and PM/Ca, to see which one works better to prepare the bowel for a colonoscopy. A colonoscopy is a test that looks inside the bowel, and a clean bowel is necessary for accurate results. The study aims to find out which laxative is more effective and easier for patients to tolerate. Participants will be randomly assigned to take one of the two laxatives before their colonoscopy, and the results will be compared to see which one works best.

This trial is for people with a condition called Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD). It involves a special kind of transplant called an autologous stem cell transplant, which uses your own stem cells to help reset your immune system. The goal is to stop the disease from getting worse and to help you go into long-term remission. To be eligible, you must be between 18 and 65 years old and have a confirmed diagnosis of NMOSD. The treatment involves several steps, including chemotherapy, medications to suppress your immune system, and the return of your own stem cells. The researchers will monitor your progress to see if the treatment is effective in stopping the disease from progressing.

This study aims to create a large database of medical information to help improve the diagnosis and treatment of lung cancer, tuberculosis, and COVID-19. The database will include electronic medical records, images, and other clinical information from patients with these conditions, as well as from healthy individuals. The goal is to use artificial intelligence to analyze this data and develop a system that can provide personalized and accurate diagnoses and predictions of treatment outcomes. To be eligible, participants must be at least 18 years old, have a confirmed diagnosis of one of these conditions or be healthy, and have complete medical records. The study will help researchers develop new technologies to improve patient care and outcomes.

This trial is studying the effectiveness of a chemotherapy drug called irofulven in treating patients with non-small cell lung cancer that has come back or didn't respond to previous treatment. Patients will receive the drug through an IV for 5 days, and this cycle will be repeated every 28 days. The goal is to see how well the drug works, how long it takes for the disease to come back, and any side effects that may occur. To be eligible, patients must be at least 18 years old, have a certain type of lung cancer, and have had previous chemotherapy. The trial aims to enroll 66 patients and will follow them for at least a year to see how they respond to the treatment.

This study is looking at the effectiveness of a lower dose of a steroid medication called betamethasone in preventing breathing problems in babies born between 34 and 36 weeks of pregnancy. The medication is usually given to pregnant women at risk of preterm birth to help their babies' lungs develop. In this study, women will be randomly assigned to receive either the usual dose or a lower dose of betamethasone. The goal is to see if the lower dose is just as effective as the usual dose in preventing breathing problems in babies born early. The study aims to help doctors determine the best way to use this medication to keep babies healthy.

This study is testing a shorter version of a therapy called Mindfulness-Based Therapy (MBT) to help people with anxiety and depression. The traditional MBT program can be very time-consuming, requiring over 30 hours of therapy sessions and 45-60 minutes of daily homework. The new, abbreviated version of MBT requires less than 10 hours of therapy sessions and less than 10 hours of homework. The goal is to see if this shorter version is still effective in reducing symptoms of anxiety and depression, and improving overall well-being. If it is, it could help more people access mental health care by reducing wait times and making therapy more accessible.

This study looks at how two different diets affect the bacteria in your gut and your overall heart health. If you're 50 or older, generally healthy, and eat a meat-based diet, you might be eligible to participate. The study involves eating controlled meals and providing samples for testing. You'll need to be willing to follow the study's rules, including not taking certain medications or supplements, and attending in-person visits. The goal is to understand how diet affects your gut health and heart wellness.

This study is looking at whether a high dose of a medication called dexamethasone, given before emergency surgery, can help reduce inflammation and improve recovery in patients with intestinal obstruction or a perforated intestine. The study will compare the effects of dexamethasone to a placebo in patients undergoing emergency laparotomy surgery. The goal is to see if dexamethasone can reduce the body's inflammatory response, improve pain management, and decrease complications after surgery. Patients will be randomly assigned to receive either dexamethasone or a placebo before surgery, and their progress will be closely monitored for several days after the operation.

This study is for people with a type of bladder cancer called urothelial bladder carcinoma that has grown into the muscle layer of the bladder. Patients in this study will receive a medication called pembrolizumab for 9 weeks before having surgery to remove their bladder. The goal of the study is to see if the pembrolizumab helps reduce the size of the tumor before surgery. Patients will have scans and tests before and after surgery to check the status of their cancer. The study is looking for people who are 18 years or older, have not had certain other treatments for their bladder cancer, and are able to have surgery.

This study is testing a new mobile phone app called My IBD Care to see if it can help people with inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn's and ulcerative colitis manage their condition better. The app allows patients to track their symptoms, access their care plan, and communicate with their healthcare team remotely. The goal is to reduce the number of hospital appointments and make it easier for patients to manage their condition, while also reducing costs for the healthcare system. The study is looking for patients aged 16-80 who have had a stable diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease for at least 6 months and have a smartphone.

This trial is comparing two surgical methods for treating colorectal cancer that has spread to the liver. Patients with this condition will be randomly assigned to have either a traditional open surgery or a less invasive surgery that combines laparoscopy with a small incision. The goal is to see which method has better short-term results after surgery. To be eligible, patients must have colorectal cancer that can be removed, liver metastasis that can be treated, and no other serious health issues. The study aims to find out which surgical approach is safer and more effective for patients with this type of cancer.

This study is looking at how well a medication called FG-4592 works to treat anemia (low red blood cell count) in people with a condition called myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). To be in the study, you must be at least 18 years old, have a certain type of MDS, and have anemia. You also cannot have had certain treatments or transfusions recently. The study will last about 30 weeks, and you will be given the medication for 26 weeks. The goal is to see if FG-4592 can help improve anemia in people with lower-risk MDS.

This study looks at how gum disease affects people with diabetes and whether treating gum disease can help improve diabetes outcomes. Researchers will survey 200 people with diabetes and collect information about their oral health, diabetes history, and overall health. A smaller group of 24 participants with gum disease will receive treatment and have their blood sugar levels and other health markers checked before and after treatment. The goal is to better understand the connection between gum disease and diabetes, and to find ways to reduce complications and improve health outcomes for people with diabetes.

This study looks at how acupuncture affects heart rate variability in people with multiple sclerosis (MS). It involves 80 participants, 40 with MS and 40 without, who will receive either real or fake acupuncture sessions over several weeks. The goal is to see how acupuncture impacts the autonomic nervous system, which controls heart rate, in people with MS. To participate, you must be at least 18 years old, have MS, and be able to understand and agree to the study. If you have certain heart conditions or a pacemaker, you may not be eligible.

This study is testing a new combination of treatments for people with advanced or metastatic cancer of the urothelial tract, which includes the bladder, urethra, ureter, or renal pelvis. The treatments being used are gemcitabine, carboplatin, and bevacizumab. Gemcitabine and carboplatin are standard chemotherapy drugs, while bevacizumab is a new type of drug that helps stop tumors from growing by cutting off their blood supply. The goal of this study is to see how well this combination of treatments works and what side effects it may cause. To be eligible, patients must be at least 18 years old, have not had chemotherapy before, and meet certain other health requirements.

This research study is looking at the safety of combining two new drugs, RAD001 and CP-751,871, to treat advanced sarcomas and other cancers. RAD001 may help stop cancer cells from growing, and CP-751,871 may help stop tumor growth. Participants will take RAD001 orally every day and receive CP-751,871 intravenously every cycle, which is 21 days. The dose of the drugs will be adjusted based on how well participants tolerate them. The goal is to find the highest dose that can be given safely without severe side effects. Participants can stay in the study as long as they don't have serious side effects or their disease doesn't get worse.

This study compares different methods for detecting tooth decay in molars, including visual exams, X-rays, and special lights. The goal is to see which method is most accurate in finding early stages of tooth decay. The study will look at 101 teeth from patients who need to have their wisdom teeth removed. The results will help dentists choose the best way to detect tooth decay and prevent further damage.

This study looks at how using a cooling helmet during open heart surgery might help protect the brain. The researchers are checking to see if the cooling helmet can reduce the level of a certain protein in the blood that is associated with brain damage, and also decrease the risk of confusion or delirium after surgery. The study involves patients who are having their first open heart surgery and are divided into two groups: one group wears the cooling helmet with cold water, and the other group wears the helmet without cold water. The researchers will take blood samples before and after surgery to check the protein levels and will also assess the patients for delirium.

This study is for patients with solid tumors that can be removed with surgery. It's looking at how well a drug called O6-benzylguanine works when given before surgery to help make the tumor easier to remove. Patients will receive a single dose of the drug and then have surgery 16-20 hours later. The goal is to find the lowest dose of the drug that can effectively reduce the tumor's activity. Patients will be followed for a few weeks after surgery to see how they're doing.

This study aims to understand how often infections occur after surgery for stomach or colon cancer in China. Researchers from 17 hospitals will collect information about patients who have this type of surgery, including their age, medical history, and any complications that happen after surgery. The goal is to gather information from 4000 patients over one year to help doctors better understand and prevent infections after surgery.

This study is comparing two groups of patients who are having open gastrointestinal surgery to see if injecting a local anesthetic called Bupivacaine into the surgical wound can help reduce pain and the risk of infection. One group will receive the Bupivacaine injection, while the other group will receive a saline solution. All patients will receive standard care to prevent infection, including antibiotics and careful wound cleaning. The study will follow patients for 30 days after surgery to see how they recover and if they develop any complications. The goal is to find out if the Bupivacaine injection is effective in reducing pain and infection risk in patients having this type of surgery.

This study aims to develop a new way to assess swallowing problems in newborns and infants using video analysis with artificial intelligence. The goal is to create a more accurate and easier method to evaluate swallowing disorders, which are common in premature babies and can be caused by various factors. Researchers will videotape babies during bottle feeding and use computer algorithms to analyze their facial features related to swallowing. The study hopes to find a correlation between the evaluation results and the baby's future development. To participate, babies must be under 6 months old, have suspected swallowing problems, and have parental consent. Babies with certain medical conditions, such as cardiopulmonary instability, or those with head and neck abnormalities may not be eligible.

This study looks at tissue samples from patients with a type of blood cancer called T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). Researchers want to understand how certain genetic changes, specifically in the NOTCH1 gene, affect the behavior of cancer cells. By studying these samples, doctors hope to learn more about what causes T-ALL and find new ways to treat it. The study will analyze 48 samples from patients with T-ALL to see how the NOTCH1 gene is involved in the disease.

This study is looking at a new way to help manage pain from broken ribs in the emergency department. Broken ribs are a common injury that can be very painful and can lead to serious complications, especially in older patients. The usual treatment for broken ribs is pain medication, but this can have side effects like constipation, nausea, and addiction. The study is testing a procedure called a serratus anterior plane block, which uses a special kind of numbing medicine to block pain in the chest area. The goal is to see if this procedure can help reduce pain and improve breathing in patients with broken ribs, and if it's a safe and effective alternative to traditional pain medication.

This study is for patients who need a procedure called an ERCP to look at and treat problems in their bile duct. Sometimes, it's hard to access the bile duct, and the doctor's tools might accidentally go into the nearby pancreatic duct instead. This study is comparing two ways to help get into the bile duct when this happens. One way is to leave a wire in the pancreatic duct and try to insert another wire into the bile duct. The other way is to make a small cut in the muscle that controls the flow of juices from the pancreas and liver, which can help guide the wire into the bile duct. The goal is to find out which method is safer and more effective in getting into the bile duct with fewer attempts, which can reduce the risk of pancreatitis, a potentially serious complication.

This study is looking at how stress affects people with systemic sclerosis, a condition that affects the skin and internal organs. The study will include 150 people with systemic sclerosis who will be divided into three groups. One group will receive online cognitive behavioral therapy to help manage stress, another group will receive education about stress and its effects, and the third group will continue with their usual care. The study will look at how these different approaches affect quality of life, stress levels, and overall well-being. Participants will complete online questionnaires and provide a hair sample to measure cortisol levels, a hormone related to stress. The goal of the study is to understand how stress impacts people with systemic sclerosis and to find effective ways to manage it.

This study looks at how well the flu vaccine works in people with major depressive disorder (MDD) and how their immune system responds to the vaccine. The study will compare people with MDD to those without the condition. Participants will receive the flu vaccine and have blood tests and brain scans to see how their body responds to the vaccine. The goal is to understand how MDD affects the immune system and how it might impact the effectiveness of the flu vaccine. The study is open to people between 18 and 55 years old, and participants will be asked to complete several visits and tests over a few weeks.

This clinical trial was designed to test the safety and effectiveness of a combination of two medications, blinatumomab and pembrolizumab, in adults with a type of cancer called diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that has come back or hasn't responded to previous treatments. The trial had two parts: the first part was to find the highest dose of blinatumomab that could be safely given with pembrolizumab, and the second part was to see how well this combination worked. However, based on the results from the first part, the decision was made not to proceed with the second part. The trial was looking for people with this type of cancer who had already tried other treatments and had a certain level of physical functioning. The goal was to see if this combination of medications could help control the cancer and improve symptoms.

This trial is for people with a condition called gastroparesis, which causes nausea, vomiting, and other stomach problems that haven't improved with usual treatments like diet changes, medications, or surgery. The study is testing a device called the Enterra Therapy Gastric Stimulation System, which uses mild electrical pulses to help the stomach work better. The device is for people with long-term, uncontrolled nausea and vomiting from gastroparesis, and the goal is to see if it can help improve their symptoms. To be eligible, participants must be at least 18 years old, have tried other treatments that didn't work, and not be a candidate for surgery due to certain health conditions.

This study, called 'DairyHealth,' looks at how dairy foods affect people with metabolic syndrome, a group of conditions that increase the risk of heart disease and diabetes. The researchers want to know if certain fats and proteins found in milk, called medium-chain saturated fatty acids and whey proteins, can help improve insulin sensitivity, blood pressure, and inflammation. Sixty-four people with metabolic syndrome will be divided into four groups and given different diets to follow for 12 weeks. The diets will include varying amounts of these fats and proteins, and the researchers will monitor the participants' health to see if there are any benefits. The goal is to understand how dairy foods can be used to help prevent or treat metabolic syndrome and related health problems.

This study is testing whether using Dysport, a type of medication, can help improve wound healing and scarring after a type of skin cancer surgery called Mohs surgery. The study will involve injecting Dysport or a placebo into the muscles of the forehead before surgery, and then comparing how well the wounds heal over time. The goal is to see if Dysport can help reduce muscle tension and inflammation around the wound, which may lead to better healing and less scarring. Participants will be followed for 6 months after surgery to track their progress and any potential side effects.

This study is looking at the best way to help people with acute decompensated heart failure get rid of excess fluid in their body. The researchers want to see if using ultrasound to look at the inferior vena cava (a large vein that carries blood to the heart) can help guide treatment and improve symptoms. Participants will be divided into two groups: one group will have their treatment guided by ultrasound and clinical assessment, and the other group will have their treatment guided by clinical assessment alone. The study will follow participants for 6-7 months to see how they do. The goal is to find out if using ultrasound can help people with heart failure feel better and reduce their risk of complications.

This trial is studying whether using ultrasound to check the lungs after thoracic surgery can help doctors decide when it's safe to send patients home after their chest drain is removed. Normally, a chest X-ray is done to check for any problems, but ultrasound is a quicker, cheaper, and safer alternative that doesn't use radiation. The study will compare the results of ultrasound and chest X-ray to see if ultrasound can be used to make discharge decisions.

This study looks at whether eating two raw tomatoes a day for a month can help increase levels of 'good' cholesterol, also known as high density lipoprotein-cholesterol (HDL-c), in people with low HDL-c levels. The study includes men and women between 18 and 65 years old who have low HDL-c levels and are otherwise healthy. Participants will be randomly assigned to either eat two tomatoes a day or a similar amount of cucumber, and their cholesterol levels will be measured before and after the study. The goal is to see if eating tomatoes can help improve HDL-c levels, which can help reduce the risk of heart disease.

This study looks at how first-year radiology residents feel when they start taking emergency room calls on their own, and compares their anxiety levels to how they feel when they take calls with an experienced resident for support. The goal is to understand how these different approaches affect residents' anxiety and well-being.

This study is looking at the best way to help preterm babies with breathing problems stop using a special machine called nasal CPAP. The goal is to find a method that allows babies to breathe on their own sooner and spend less time in the hospital. The study is for preterm babies born between 28 and 37 weeks of gestation who are having trouble breathing. Researchers want to see which method of stopping nasal CPAP works best for these babies.

This trial is for people with type 2 diabetes who are taking metformin as their only diabetes treatment. The study will test how a new oral medication, AR-C165395XX, works in the body over 3 days. Participants will take either the new medication or a placebo, and their blood sugar levels will be monitored. To be eligible, participants must be at least 18 years old, have a body mass index between 19 and 38, and have a certain level of blood sugar control. The study aims to understand how the new medication affects the body and to check for any potential side effects.

This study is looking at how a single dose of green coffee extract affects blood sugar levels in healthy adults. Green coffee extract has been shown to have benefits for glucose metabolism and weight management, but most studies have looked at its long-term effects. The researchers want to see if taking green coffee extract with other natural substances, like alpha-lipoic acid or dihydroberberine, can help control blood sugar levels after consuming a sugary drink. They are looking for healthy adults aged 18-45 to participate in the study.

This study is looking for a low-cost and effective way to teach microsurgical skills to beginners. Researchers will compare four different models, including Japanese shirataki konjac noodles, to see which one is best for learning. Participants, who are either surgical residents or individuals with no microsurgical experience, will practice performing a specific surgical task on each model and provide feedback on their experience. The goal is to find a model that is easy to use, cost-effective, and helpful for learning microsurgical skills, which can be used in educational programs for surgeons around the world.

This study is testing whether using telemedicine (remote healthcare through technology) can help improve the care of patients with chronic kidney disease who are using a type of dialysis called peritoneal dialysis. The goal is to see if telemedicine can reduce hospitalizations, unscheduled doctor visits, and costs related to complications that could have been prevented. Patients will be followed for 2 years and their medical costs, hospital visits, and complications will be tracked. The study aims to find out if using telemedicine can make it easier for patients to manage their condition and improve their overall health.

This study is looking at whether a medication called misoprostol can help reduce bleeding during a surgical abortion in the second trimester of pregnancy. Women who are 16-21 weeks pregnant and undergoing a surgical abortion will be randomly assigned to receive either misoprostol or a placebo (a dummy treatment) about an hour before the procedure. The researchers will then measure the amount of bleeding during the abortion and compare it between the two groups. They will also ask women about their pain levels and other symptoms during the procedure. The goal of the study is to see if misoprostol can help make the abortion procedure safer and more comfortable for women.

This study is looking at whether a medication called aliskiren can help reduce episodes of atrial fibrillation (irregular heartbeat) in people who have a pacemaker due to certain heart conditions. The study will use the pacemaker to track the heart's rhythm and see if aliskiren can help reduce the frequency of atrial fibrillation. To be eligible, participants must be between 18 and 85 years old, have a pacemaker, and experience irregular heartbeats. The goal of the study is to find new and safe treatments to reduce the occurrence of atrial fibrillation and related complications in people with pacemakers.

This study is looking at how different types of ketone supplements affect the body. Ketones are chemicals that can help with energy and weight loss. The study will compare how different supplements, including ones that contain ingredients like BHB and AcAc, affect ketone levels, glucose, and other health markers in healthy men aged 20-30. Participants will visit the study center several times, where they will drink a supplement and have their blood and breathing tested over a few hours. The goal is to understand how these supplements work and which ones might be most effective.

This study is looking at a new treatment called GC012F injection for people with a condition called generalized myasthenia gravis (gMG) that has not responded to other treatments. The study will check if the treatment is safe, well-tolerated, and effective. Participants will receive an infusion of GC012F after undergoing some tests and preparations. The study will also monitor participants for any side effects and track how their condition changes over time. To be eligible, participants must be at least 18 years old, have confirmed refractory gMG, and meet other specific criteria. The study aims to help researchers understand how GC012F works and if it can be a potential treatment option for people with refractory gMG.

This study is looking at how well a test called Cologuard works in people with a genetic condition called Lynch Syndrome (LS) to detect colon cancer and precancerous growths. Up to 90 people with LS will be asked to participate and will have a Cologuard test and a colonoscopy as part of their regular care. The goal is to see how well the Cologuard test compares to the colonoscopy and to understand how people with LS feel about using the Cologuard test. The results will help plan a larger study to compare the two tests.

This study looks at how well a special kind of ultrasound, called Point of Care Ultrasound (POCUS), can help doctors diagnose hip problems in children who come to the emergency room with a limp or leg pain. The study compares the results of the POCUS exam, done by a pediatric emergency doctor, to a regular ultrasound scan done by a radiologist. The goal is to see how accurate the POCUS exam is in finding out if a child has fluid in their hip joint, which can cause pain and limping. Children aged 0-18 who come to the emergency room with a limp or leg pain, but without any trauma or obvious diagnosis, can participate in the study.

This study is looking at how two HIV medications, etravirine and darunavir/ritonavir, interact with an antimalarial medication called artemether/lumefantrine in healthy people. The goal is to see if taking these medications together affects how they work in the body. The study will involve 32 healthy participants who will take the medications in different combinations and have their blood levels checked to see how the medications are absorbed and eliminated. The study is looking for healthy people between the ages of 18 and 55 who do not have HIV and are not pregnant or breastfeeding. Participants will need to use effective birth control and not smoke for at least 3 months before the study.

This study is looking at whether a treatment called remote ischemic preconditioning (RIPC) can help protect patients from complications during and after a procedure called carotid artery stenting. RIPC involves briefly restricting and then restoring blood flow to the arms to help prepare the body for the procedure. The study will compare patients who receive RIPC, a sham version of RIPC, or no RIPC before their procedure to see if RIPC can reduce the risk of brain injury, inflammation, and other complications. Patients will be followed to see how they do after the procedure and whether RIPC has any long-term benefits.

This study is looking at how well acupuncture works to help people with gastrointestinal tract and lung cancers who have lost their appetite. Researchers will divide 160 participants into three groups to compare the effects of acupuncture, a medication called Megestrol acetate, and a placebo. The study will check how these treatments affect appetite over 15 days and monitor any side effects. To be eligible, participants must be at least 18 years old, have a certain level of appetite loss, and have lost weight in the past six months. The goal is to see if acupuncture is a safe and effective way to improve appetite in people with these types of cancers.

This study is for people with type 1 diabetes who use an insulin pump and a device to continuously monitor their blood sugar levels. The goal is to see how using a 'closed-loop' system, which automatically adjusts insulin levels, affects their quality of life and how they feel about managing their diabetes. Participants will complete questionnaires and have their blood sugar levels monitored over 6 months. The study aims to understand how this new technology impacts people with type 1 diabetes and if it can improve their overall well-being.

This study is for people with actinic keratosis, a skin condition caused by too much sun exposure. The goal is to see how a special gel, called SR-T100, works in the body. The gel contains a substance called solamargine, which comes from a plant extract. Participants will apply the gel to a small area of skin and then have blood tests done over 36 hours to see how the substance is absorbed. The study will also check for any side effects. To be eligible, participants must be at least 20 years old and have actinic keratosis lesions in a specific area of skin. They cannot have used certain treatments or medications in the past few weeks or have certain other skin conditions.
